title: Pricey Walmart Stock Falls More Often, Not Harder
detail:
Pricey Walmart Stock Falls More Often, Not Harder
Trefis Team

Image from Pixabay

Walmart reports its third quarter tomorrow, Thursday, Nov 19, before the market opens. Most previews will ask what its holiday outlook says about the shopper. This article asks a narrower question. Does Walmart stock fall harder on report day when it starts out expensive?

The short answer is no, not harder. But it has fallen more often when it starts at 40 times earnings or more. Across 31 reports since Feb 2019, the link between the starting price-to-earnings multiple and the report-day move is close to zero. The biggest fall, 11.4% in May 2022, came at 30.4 times earnings, in the middle of the range. Yet the last three reports all started above 40 times earnings, and the stock fell after each one.

That matters now. Walmart closed at $127.52 on Tuesday. That is 46.0 times its earnings over the past four quarters. Only three past reports started at a higher multiple.

How We Measured Each Report Day

The price-to-earnings multiple, or P/E, is the share price divided by a year of earnings per share. We used earnings per share under standard accounting rules, called GAAP, for the four quarters before each report. The report-day move runs from the close before the release to the close on report day. Walmart released all 31 reports before the market opened. Prices before the stock split on Feb 26, 2024 are divided by three.

Over the whole record, the stock fell on 16 report days and rose on 15. The average move in either direction was 3.9%. Up or down has been close to an even split.

Three Groups, Sorted By Starting Multiple

We sorted the 31 reports by starting P/E and cut them into three groups. The table shows how each group did.

August 2026 started at 40.1 times, so it falls in the middle group. The middle group had the deepest average fall, 6.2%. It includes the worst day, in May 2022. The most expensive group fell 3.8% on an average down day. By this cut, expensive starts did not produce bigger drops.

The difference shows up in the average move. The cheapest group gained 0.7% on an average report day. The most expensive group lost 1.0%. A split at 40 times earnings, which also takes in August 2026, points the same way. Reports at 40 times or more averaged a 1.7% loss. Reports below that line averaged a 0.7% gain. Above the line, the stock fell on 7 of 12 report days. Below it, the stock fell on 9 of 19.

That second cut also makes the falls look a little larger at high multiples. The average fall was 4.6% at 40 times or more and 3.7% below it. So the size of the falls depends on where you draw the line. The direction of the average move does not.

title: Anthropic’s unusual IPO comes at a fragile time for AI and Wall Street
detail:
Anthropic’s unusual IPO comes at a fragile time for AI and Wall Street
Stan Choe
Wed, November 18, 2026 at 2:09 PM MST 5 min read
ANT
WMT
Trade Walmart on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
People protest artificial intelligence and data centers ahead of a New York City Council Committee hearing on the risks and regulation of artificial intelligence, at City Hall Park on October 05, 2026 in New York City (Getty Images)

As Anthropic prepares to list its stock for the first time later this week, the launch represents a significant trial not just for the maker of the Claude AI chatbot, but for the wider artificial-intelligence sector and the U.S. equity market.

The company's initial public offering will carry consequences well past tech enthusiasts who grasp its framework as a "public benefit corporation." Its impact is likely to reach individuals who make zero adjustments to their 401(k) retirement portfolios.

Here's a look at what investors should know ahead of the highly anticipated IPO:

Anthropic will instantly become one of Wall Street's biggest stocks

Anthropic is planning to sell shares of its stock for between $70 and $78 apiece, which would likely give it a total value of more than $1 trillion.

Such a size would rival Walmart, which has more than 10,900 stores around the world, and JPMorgan Chase, whose roots go back to 1799. It would also be more valuable than Coca-Cola, IBM, Starbucks, Delta Air Lines and General Motors — combined.

Investors could end up owning Anthropic, even without buying any shares

At that size, Anthropic could quickly join indexes that track wide swaths of the stock market, which in turn could bring in even more investment.

Anthropic could join the Nasdaq 100 index within just a few weeks, for example. The index tracks the 100 largest nonfinancial companies trading on the Nasdaq, and it's a popular way for investors to get a quick read on how tech stocks are doing generally.

Co-founder and CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei at the White House in Washington, DC, on September 29, 2026 (AFP via Getty Images)

The index is so popular that an exchange-traded fund that mimics it, Invesco's QQQ ETF, has roughly $457 billion invested in it. If Anthropic joins the index, QQQ and other funds tracking the Nasdaq 100 would automatically buy Anthropic stock.

It would take longer for Anthropic to join the more widely followed S&P 500 index, though. To enter that index, a stock needs to have traded for at least 12 months, among other criteria.

Investors buying Anthropic stock will have less control of it than is typical

The goal of most companies, above all, is to do well for their owners. Usually, that means making profits and growing, both in the short and long terms.

Anthropic says it too will consider its stockholders, but it will balance their interests against another fundamental goal: "the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."

As part of that, Anthropic has set up a long-term benefit trust that will have the ability to elect or remove a majority of the company's board of directors. This trust will not run the day-to-day operations of Anthropic. But its influence means the company could opt for strategies that may not make the most money for investors in the long term.

title: An $11 Billion Fund Dumps These 3 Stocks
detail:
An $11 Billion Fund Dumps These 3 Stocks
Roxanna Maglangit

WMT

Trading disclosure
An $11 Billion Fund Dumps These 3 Stocks ©12963734 from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Junto Capital Management, which manages $10.52 billion, sold out of Walmart, Visa and Moody's in the third quarter, its latest 13F shows.

Walmart trades at about 43x forward earnings with 3% upside to the analysts' average target, which makes that sale the easiest to agree with.

By Sept. 30, the fund's two biggest holdings were BlackRock and Ferguson Enterprises, where analysts see 16% and 17% upside.

Visa trades near its long-run multiple with earnings still growing at a double-digit pace, so it's the sale I'd most want to undo.

Junto Capital Management's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 16, shows the fund sold out of 13 sizable positions. The three biggest are stocks plenty of investors own: Walmart (WMT:NASDAQ), Visa (V:NYSE) and Moody's (MCO:NYSE).

Junto manages $10.52 billion in all, per its latest Form ADV, and its 13F holds $5.63 billion of US stocks across 80 positions. By Sept. 30, the top of that list was BlackRock (BLK:NYSE), after the fund added 35% to its stake, followed by Ferguson Enterprises (FERG:NYSE), new in the quarter.

Walmart's price already asks a lot

Junto held 1.49 million Walmart shares worth $168 million on June 30, 3.1% of its 13F stocks, and none by Sept. 30. The stock has gained 13% since the quarter ended. The analysts' average target has climbed over the past year, though it's below its June high:

Walmart (WMT): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

That $131.90 average, from 44 analysts, is just 3% above the price. At about 43x forward earnings, Walmart trades far above its five-year average of about 29x on TIKR. At that average, analysts' fiscal 2029 EPS estimate of $3.63 would be worth about $107 a share. Meanwhile, Walmart is putting the roughly $2.9 billion of tariff refunds it booked in its fiscal second quarter into more than 11,000 rollbacks, and it guides third-quarter adjusted operating income up just 2% to 4% in constant currency. That's a rich price for profit growth that slow.

TIKR tracks 45 analysts on Walmart. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Walmart, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Walmart's Analyst Ratings

Visa is the sale I'd question

Visa was a similar-sized position: 461,921 shares worth $158 million on June 30, 2.9% of its 13F stocks. It's up 21% since Sept. 30, and the analysts' average target has climbed to its highest point of the past year:

Visa (V): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

Even after that run, the $449.06 average from 40 analysts sits 8% above the price. Visa trades at about 28x forward earnings, right around its quarter-end average since 2014 on TIKR. Analysts expect normalized EPS to grow from $15.02 in fiscal 2027 to $17.13 in fiscal 2028. Visa also just raised its dividend 16%. And Pershing Square's Bill Ackman told CNBC this month that he bought Visa this year, calling it "a royalty on people spending money."

Not everyone agrees. Freedom Broker cut Visa to Hold from Buy on Nov. 4, pointing to rising client incentives, even as it raised its target to $427 from $410. The bigger risk is the Credit Card Competition Act. President Trump has backed it, and it would let merchants send credit card payments over rival networks.

Moody's is the closest call

Moody's was the smallest of the three: 260,298 shares worth $118 million on June 30, 2.2% of its 13F stocks. It's up 7% since Sept. 30 and still 11% below its 52-week high. Its average target has stayed between $533 and $576 all year:

Moody's (MCO): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

That $553.67 average from 24 analysts is 14% above the price, the most upside of the three, and even the lowest target, $480, is about where the stock trades. Growth has slowed, though. In its third-quarter release on Oct. 21, Moody's said revenue rose 1% to $2.02 billion, and ratings revenue fell 1%. That came after 15% revenue growth in the second quarter. Moody's still reaffirmed its 2026 guidance, including adjusted EPS of $16.50 to $17.00. At about 27x forward earnings, it costs about what Visa does, for a business that's growing more slowly right now.

Its two biggest holdings look cheaper

The top of Junto's 13F looks a lot cheaper than the three stocks it sold. By Sept. 30, BlackRock was its largest position: 191,489 shares worth $203 million, 3.6% of its 13F stocks, after a 35% jump in its share count over the quarter. Ferguson Enterprises, new in the quarter, came second at 778,403 shares worth $173 million, 3.1%. Both are up 12% since Sept. 30, and analysts still see 16% upside in BlackRock and 17% in Ferguson. At about 19x and 20x forward earnings, both trade far below Walmart's multiple, and below Visa's and Moody's too.

If I could buy one back, it's Visa

Selling Walmart at 43x looks like the easiest of the three calls, and I wouldn't argue hard over Moody's. I'd part ways with Junto on Visa. I'd rather own a business with double-digit earnings growth at its usual multiple, so if I could only buy back one of the three right now, it'd be Visa.

Walmart reports on Nov. 19. That sale would look early if adjusted EPS lands at the top of the $0.62-$0.64 guide or better, with Walmart U.S. comparable sales excluding health and wellness at 3% or more. Junto's next 13F, for the quarter ending Dec. 31, is due by mid-February. It'll show whether the fund bought any of the three back.

title: Should You Buy Walmart Stock Before Nov. 19? History Has a Clear Answer.
detail:
Should You Buy Walmart Stock Before Nov. 19? History Has a Clear Answer.
Micah Zimmerman, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 18, 2026 at 12:11 PM MST 5 min read
WMT
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Pop quiz: What did Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT) stock do the last four times the company reported earnings?

If you guessed "went up, because it's Walmart," you're one for four. Shares jumped about 6.5% after the November 2025 report, slipped about 1.4% in February, dropped about 7% in May, and tumbled about 9% in August.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Walmart reports again before the opening bell on Thursday, Nov. 19, with results due around 7 a.m. ET and a call with management an hour later. So should you buy before then? History gives a pretty clear answer -- just not the one you might expect.

Image source: Getty Images.

Four earnings days, one coin flip

Those four reactions had more to do with the forecast than the quarter. In May, sales beat expectations, but cautious guidance amid soaring gas prices sent shares lower. In August, Walmart raised its full-year outlook and still fell as Wall Street fixated on weaker-than-expected U.S. same-store sales. Walmart tends to lowball that forecast, too. After February's soft outlook, Baird analyst Peter Benedict pointed to the company's "history of conservatism."

Thursday's bar is high. Shares trade at about 46 times earnings and sit near their 52-week high after climbing about 7% in the past month. That's a rich P/E ratio, and CFO John David Rainey noted in August that Walmart was absorbing more than $2 billion in extra fuel costs "in arguably a softer consumer environment."

Zoom out, though, and those scary drops shrink fast. Someone who bought two days before August's plunge is still ahead today, and shares are up about 26% from a week before last November's report.

The longer view says the same thing. In its latest annual report, Walmart showed that $100 invested in February 2021, with dividends reinvested, grew to about $272 by early 2026, versus about $201 for the S&P 500. The interesting part is that the first two years were dull, with that $100 worth only about $106 by early 2023. That's the trouble with market timing. The payoff often shows up while you're not looking.

Walmart has also raised its dividend for 53 straight years. This move of over 50 straight years of raises makes it a Dividend King.

The business under the coin flip

What keeps me interested is what Walmart actually does in the 90-odd days between earnings reports. Furner, a three-decade Walmart veteran, took over as CEO on Feb. 1, and he's betting on speed. "Speed isn't simply a fulfillment metric; it's an acquisition strategy," he said in August, adding that fast-delivery customers shop more often and are more likely to join Walmart+.

The newest piece arrives by air. On Nov. 5, Walmart agreed to add 300 Zipline drone delivery sites nationwide. "We see customers try drone delivery for the novelty and then continue to come back to it for the convenience," said Greg Cathey, who leads Walmart's e-commerce fulfillment transformation.

Walmart is also quietly making money on a lot more than groceries. Its advertising business, which includes Walmart Connect and Vizio, and its memberships both continued to grow last quarter. "The math isn't simply one plus one equals two," Furner said of how those businesses feed each other.

Then there's artificial intelligence. Walmart already sells through ChatGPT, Google's Gemini, and others, and it's rolling out Agent Profiles that let shoppers set a spending limit for an AI agent. "We price products, not people," the company wrote, promising agents see the same prices humans do. This holiday season, its Sparky assistant can even make an item's shelf tag light up in the store so you can find it.

So, should you buy Walmart stock before Nov. 19? History says the date barely matters. If you're buying just to catch a pop, the last four reports say you're flipping a coin. If you want to own Walmart for the next decade, buy when you're ready, maybe in pieces, so a rough Thursday becomes a chance to add more instead of a reason to panic.

title: Buy the Spike in Target (TGT) Stock After Strong Q3 Earnings?
detail:
Buy the Spike in Target (TGT) Stock After Strong Q3 Earnings?
Shaun Pruitt
Wed, November 18, 2026 at 12:52 PM MST 2 min read
TGT
NVDA
WMT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Shares of retail giant Target TGT) have surged as much as 7% in Wednesday's trading session after delivering stronger-than-expected Q3 results and guidance, making the company a bright spot in this week's highly anticipated earnings lineup.

This comes as turmoil around Nvidia's NVDA) leadership transition has overshadowed its impressive quarterly results, while investors await Walmart's WMT) Q3 report on Thursday for further insight into consumer spending trends.

With Target stock gaining momentum and now up 75% year to date, let's examine whether its latest earnings beat and upbeat outlook make TGT a compelling buy.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Target's Strong Q3 Results

Target reported Q3 adjusted earnings of $2.65 per share, surging 49% year over year and crushing Wall Street expectations of $2.05 by 29%.

Notably, Q3 earnings benefited from $0.50 per share in tariff refunds, although adjusted EPS still increased 21% YoY to $2.15 excluding this benefit and reflected a nearly 5% earnings surprise.

Quarterly sales rose 7% to $27.07 billion, exceeding estimates of $26.36 billion. Encouragingly, comparable sales increased over 5%, driven by a 5% rise in customer traffic, with digital comparable sales jumping nearly 10%. Strength in electronics, beauty, and food and beverage helped drive broad-based growth.

It's also noteworthy that Target's gross margin expanded to 30.5% from 28.2% a year ago, with margins still improving by approximately 120 basis points excluding tariff refunds.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Target Raises FY26 Guidance

More importantly, Target raised its full-year sales growth outlook to approximately 6%, up from its previous forecast of 5%.

Management also increased its adjusted EPS guidance to $10.65-$11.40 (+40% YoY growth), compared with its prior projection of $9.90-$10.90. However, the updated outlook includes approximately $2.14 per share in tariff refund benefits recognized this year.

Looking ahead, Target expects to invest $5-$6 billion in capital expenditures during 2027 to support sustained growth, while improving sales trends heading into the critical holiday shopping season provide additional optimism.

Bottom Line: Is TGT Stock Still a Buy?

Benefiting from a trend of positive earnings estimate revisions that could extend following its impressive Q3 report and raised guidance, Target looks well-positioned to retain its Zacks Rank #2 (Buy).

While the contribution from tariff refunds warrants some caution, Target's strengthening underlying sales trends and improving outlook support its investment appeal even after Wednesday's rally.

title: Walmart Or Amazon: Which Is The Tech Stock Now?

Walmart Or Amazon: Which Is The Tech Stock Now?

Today's big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?

Walmart reports quarterly results on Thursday, Nov 19, before the market opens. The results come out at 7 a.m. ET. Investors will read them for what shoppers bought, what they paid, and whether they will keep spending through the holidays.

The bigger story is the stock's price. At Tuesday's close, investors paid 46 times Walmart's profit over the last year. For Amazon, they paid 21 times. This measure is the trailing price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E: the share price divided by the last four quarters' profit per share. On it, the grocer is priced like a tech company, and the tech company like a grocer.

Is Walmart Growing Like A Tech Company?

No, and that is the puzzle. Walmart's sales grew 5.9% in its latest quarter from a year earlier. Amazon's grew 12.1%. Amazon also keeps more of each sale. Over the last four quarters, it kept 13.1 cents of every sales dollar as operating profit, the profit from running the business. Walmart kept 4.4 cents.

So Walmart's 46 times buys a slower business with thinner margins than Amazon's. Among the four stocks below, only Costco costs more, at 53 times. Target costs 17 times.

Walmart's 46 times is a growth price for a business growing slower than Amazon's. Most portfolios settle for growth or for income. The Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio is built for growth: more than 105% since September 2020. The Trefis Income Solution is built for income, with a dividend yield about 3x the S&P 500's. We'd be glad to show you both: see the HQ Portfolio or see the Income Solution.

Two caveats. First, Amazon's 21 times flatters it. In the quarter to June, Amazon booked $62.6 billion of profit on $27.5 billion of operating income. The gap came from outside its operations. Measured against operating income, Walmart still costs 31.4 times and Amazon 26.7 times.

Second, the forward P/E uses analysts' estimates of next year's profit. On that basis, Walmart costs about 40 times and Amazon 24 times. Analysts also expect Amazon's sales to grow about 15% a year through 2030. For Walmart, they expect about 4%.

What Is The Market Paying For?

Investors are paying for the direction of Walmart's margin, not its level. Its operating margin was 5.0% in the July quarter, up from 4.1% a year earlier. That rise was helped by tariff refunds Walmart says it will put back into prices. Delivery, advertising and membership fees are making the grocer look more like a platform.
